features.name: projected_final_load_deficit
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Deficit of a machine's post-placement load below the projected final average load."""
    m = len(loads)
    mean_past = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size > 0 else float(job)
    # projected total work = assigned so far + this job + expected remaining work
    target = (float(loads.sum()) + float(job) + float(jobs_left) * mean_past) / m
    denom = abs(target) + abs(float(job)) + 1e-9
    vals = (target - (loads + float(job))) / denom
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=-1.0), -1.0, 1.0)
features.measures: Deficit of a machine's post-placement load below the projected final average load.

features.name: best_fit_below_max
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative distance between the job size and each machine's headroom below the current maximum load (best-fit packing under the max)."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    job = float(job)
    if loads.size == 0:
        return np.zeros(0, dtype=float)
    max_load = float(np.max(loads))
    slack = max_load - loads
    scale = max(max_load, job) + 1e-9
    return -np.abs(slack - job) / scale
features.measures: Negative distance between the job size and each machine's headroom below the current maximum load (best-fit packing under the max).

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Minus the absolute deviation of each machine's load from the mean load, scaled by (max load + job)."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    if loads.size == 0:
        return loads
    mean_load = float(loads.mean())
    peak = float(loads.max())
    denom = peak + float(job) + 1e-9
    return -np.abs(loads - mean_load) / denom

features.name: least_load_plus_fill_to_predicted_target
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Two columns: (1) negative current load (least-loaded rule); (2) negative distance from load+job to the predicted final per-machine load, estimated from observed mean job size and the number of jobs still to arrive."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    job = float(job)
    m = loads.size

    total_seen = float(past_jobs.sum()) + job          # work of all jobs seen so far, incl. this one
    count = int(past_jobs.size) + 1
    mean_job = total_seen / count
    est_total = total_seen + jobs_left * mean_job      # expected total work of the whole instance
    target = est_total / m                             # per-machine share of that estimate

    maxload = loads.max()
    after = loads + job
    scale = maxload + job + target + 1e-9              # keeps both columns in about [-1, 1]

    col0 = -loads / scale
    col1 = -np.abs(after - target) / scale             # fill toward (but not past) the predicted final load
    return np.stack([col0, col1], axis=1)
features.measures: Two columns: (1) negative current load (least-loaded rule); (2) negative distance from load+job to the predicted final per-machine load, estimated from observed mean job size and the number of jobs still to arrive.

features.name: reserve_emptiest_machine_for_big_jobs
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """For a small job: prefers a machine a little above the emptiest, keeping the emptiest free for a future big job; for a big job: plain least-loaded."""
    eps = 1e-9
    if len(past_jobs) > 0:
        mu = float(np.mean(past_jobs))
        big = float(np.max(past_jobs))
    else:
        mu = float(job)
        big = float(job)
    mu = max(mu, eps)
    big = max(big, eps)

    lmin = float(np.min(loads))
    d = np.clip((loads - lmin) / mu, 0.0, 1e6)   # slack above the emptiest machine, in typical-job units

    # how strongly to reserve the emptiest machine: only when this job is small vs past jobs,
    # a bigger job has actually been seen, and more jobs are still coming
    if jobs_left <= 0:
        h = 0.0
    else:
        h = (mu / (mu + job)) * (big / (big + job))

    # base: prefer small load (monotone); reward: bumps a machine just above the minimum,
    # so the very emptiest machine is no longer the winner when h is large
    val = -(d / (1.0 + d)) + 2.5 * h * d * np.exp(-d)
    return np.nan_to_num(val, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=-1.0)
features.measures: For a small job: prefers a machine a little above the emptiest, keeping the emptiest free for a future big job; for a big job: plain least-loaded.

features.name: distance_to_estimated_mean_load
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative relative distance of a machine's post-assignment load from the estimated final average load."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    m = loads.shape[0]
    job = float(job)
    past = np.asarray(past_jobs, dtype=float)

    mean_job = past.mean() if past.size > 0 else job
    total = past.sum() + job + mean_job * float(jobs_left)
    target = total / m if m > 0 else job

    scale = max(abs(target), abs(job), 1.0)
    post = loads + job
    # peaks where the machine ends near the eventual mean load; both under- and over-shoot are penalised
    return -np.abs(post - target) / scale
features.measures: Negative relative distance of a machine's post-assignment load from the estimated final average load.

features.name: least_loaded_greedy
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negated projected makespan after placing the job here: -max(new_load_i, largest other load) / (max_load + job), in [-1, 0]."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    m = loads.shape[0]
    job = float(job)
    D = float(np.max(loads)) + job + 1e-9
    if D < 1e-9:
        D = 1e-9
    if m == 1:
        return np.array([-1.0])
    s = np.sort(loads)[::-1]
    top1 = float(s[0])
    top2 = float(s[1])
    is_max = loads >= top1 - 1e-12
    n_max = int(np.sum(is_max))
    other_top = top1 if n_max >= 2 else top2
    max_excl = np.where(is_max, other_top, top1)
    new_load = loads + job
    proj_max = np.maximum(new_load, max_excl)
    return -proj_max / D

idea.hypothesis: Code Zero sends every job to machine 0, so one machine carries all the work (max_machine_jobs = all jobs, spread 400-2000%). Ranking machines by negated load puts each job on the emptiest machine, which is exactly the decision that minimises the resulting max load. This is the single dominant mechanism missing from the policy.
idea.feature: m = loads.shape[0]; return -loads / (loads.max() + job + 1e-9)  # one column, shape (m,), in [-1,0]; highest score = emptiest machine; ties resolve to lowest index

features.coder_note: It computes `-loads / (loads.max() + job + 1e-9)` for each machine, so the emptiest machine scores highest (0 for empty, down to -1 for the current max), with ties broken to the lowest index by the policy's argmax; the empty-array case can't occur since m>=1, and the denominator is floored at 1e-9 …
features.measures: Negated projected makespan after placing the job here: -max(new_load_i, largest other load) / (max_load + job), in [-1, 0].

features.name: balance_to_target
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative distance of each machine's post-assignment load from the projected final fair-share level (work already present plus expected work of jobs still to come), squashed to (-1, 0]."""
    m = loads.shape[0]
    total = loads.sum() + job
    # expected size of a not-yet-seen job: mean of the ones seen so far
    if past_jobs.shape[0] > 0:
        mu = float(past_jobs.mean())
    else:
        mu = float(job)
    # level every machine must end at: current work plus expected remaining work, split evenly
    target = (total + jobs_left * mu) / m
    # experiment's scale: the largest resulting load (constant across candidates)
    scale = loads.max() + job + 1e-9
    return -np.tanh(np.abs(loads + job - target) / scale)

idea.hypothesis: Greedy in a01 only ever asks 'who is emptiest'; it never asks 'who is closest to the level everyone must end at'. If the target rule (-|load+p-(sum+p)/m|) lands loads on a common finish level, spread collapses and the tail jobs stop raising the max; if instead it concentrates work on the fullest machine (a real risk when all loads sit well below the target), the spread diagnostic will say so.
idea.feature: target = (loads.sum() + job) / loads.shape[0]; return -np.abs(loads + job - target) / (loads.max() + job + 1e-9)  # one column, in [-1,0]; machines whose resulting load is nearest the fair share score highest
idea.lesson: Champion has no features: spread is 1000% on exponential, so nothing is balancing at all yet.

features.coder_note: Measures, per machine, how close its resulting load `loads + job` is to the fair-share finish level `(sum(loads) + job) / m`, negated and divided by `max(loads) + job` (plus `1e-9`) as the experiment specifies, so nearest-to-target machines score highest; I read the scaling denominator literally as…
features.measures: Negative distance of each machine's post-assignment load from the projected final fair-share level (work already present plus expected work of jobs still to come), squashed to (-1, 0].

features.name: projected_share_overshoot_hinge
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Smooth (softplus) overshoot of a machine's resulting load above the projected final fair share, in [-1, 0]."""
    m = loads.shape[0]
    mean_past = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else float(job)
    rem = jobs_left * mean_past
    fair_final = (loads.sum() + job + rem) / m
    scale = loads.max() + job + rem / m + 1e-9
    x = (loads + job - fair_final) / scale
    sp = np.logaddexp(0.0, x)          # stable softplus, >= 0, ~0 below the share, ~x above
    return -(sp / (1.0 + sp))          # in (-1, 0], strictly decreasing in resulting load

idea.hypothesis: An even share of the remaining work (jobs_left x mean past size) is identical for every machine, so it cancels out of any 'projected final load' and cannot rank candidates by itself; the only thing jobs_left can buy is a threshold - whether a machine's resulting load overshoots the projected final fair share and so is doomed to set the makespan. This probe keeps only that hinge (0 for every machine still under the projected share), so it fires only on overshoot and lets the greedy feature choose among safe machines.
idea.feature: m = loads.shape[0]; mean_past = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else float(job); rem = jobs_left * mean_past; fair_final = (loads.sum() + job + rem) / m; scale = loads.max() + job + rem / m + 1e-9; return -np.maximum(loads + job - fair_final, 0.0) / scale  # one column, in [-1,0]; 0 for machines whose result stays at or below the projected final share, negative in proportion to the overshoot
idea.lesson: Code Zero's late_growth is 13.3% on bimodal: the tail keeps raising the makespan because nothing reserves capacity for the projected remaining work.

features.name: horizon_blended_target_fit
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Horizon-blended fit to the projected final average load: deficit below it while the run is young, two-sided distance to it when few jobs remain."""
    m = len(loads)
    t = int(past_jobs.size)
    mean_past = float(past_jobs.mean()) if t > 0 else float(job)
    # projected total work = assigned so far + this job + expected remaining work
    target = (float(loads.sum()) + float(job) + float(jobs_left) * mean_past) / m
    post = loads + float(job)
    denom = abs(target) + abs(float(job)) + 1e-9
    # share of the instance already seen, in [0, 1): 0 at the first job
    a = t / (t + float(jobs_left) + 1.0)
    deficit = (target - post) / denom            # parent: rank = least loaded
    dist = -np.abs(post - target) / denom        # late: hug the fair-share water level
    vals = (1.0 - a) * deficit + a * dist
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=-1.0), -1.0, 1.0)
features.measures: Horizon-blended fit to the projected final average load: deficit below it while the run is young, two-sided distance to it when few jobs remain.

features.name: asymmetric_level_hinge_by_job_size
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Two columns: (1) an asymmetric hinge around a level that blends the projected final per-machine share with the current bottleneck load, where the pull from below shrinks and the penalty from above grows as the arriving job gets large relative to the typical job; (2) a penalty for leaving a machine more than one typical job below that level (wasted slack)."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    job = float(job)
    m = loads.size

    # --- projected fair-share level -------------------------------------
    total = float(loads.sum()) + job
    n = int(past_jobs.size)
    if n > 0:
        mean_job = (float(past_jobs.sum()) + job) / (n + 1)
        sd_job = float(np.std(past_jobs))
    else:
        mean_job = job
        sd_job = 0.0
    mean_job = max(mean_job, 1e-9)
    sd_job = max(sd_job, 0.0)

    share = (total + float(jobs_left) * mean_job) / m
    maxload = float(loads.max())
    level = 0.5 * (share + (share if share >= maxload else maxload))
    scale = abs(level) + job + mean_job + 1e-9

    after = loads + job

    # --- column 0: size-conditioned asymmetric hinge --------------------
    big = job / (job + mean_job)                      # 0 = tiny job, 1 = huge job
    w_over = 0.5 + 0.5 * big                          # big jobs: never widen the bottleneck
    w_under = 0.5 - 0.5 * big                         # small jobs: fill toward the level
    over = np.maximum(after - level, 0.0) / scale
    under = np.maximum(level - after, 0.0) / scale
    col0 = -(w_over * over + w_under * under)

    # --- column 1: don't strand a machine far below the level -----------
    band = max(mean_job, sd_job)                      # one typical job of tolerable slack
    col1 = -np.maximum((level - band) - after, 0.0) / scale

    out = np.stack([col0, col1], axis=1)
    out = np.nan_to_num(out, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=-1.0)
    return np.clip(out, -1.0, 1.0)
features.measures: Two columns: (1) an asymmetric hinge around a level that blends the projected final per-machine share with the current bottleneck load, where the pull from below shrinks and the penalty from above grows as the arriving job gets large relative to the typical job; (2) a penalty for leaving a machine more than one typical job below that level (wasted slack).

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative absolute log-ratio between a machine's post-assignment load and the projected final average load (relative rather than absolute distance)."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    m = loads.shape[0]
    job = float(job)
    past = np.asarray(past_jobs, dtype=float)

    mean_job = float(past.mean()) if past.size > 0 else job
    total = float(loads.sum()) + job + mean_job * float(jobs_left)
    target = max(total / float(max(m, 1)), 1e-9)

    post = np.maximum(loads + job, 1e-9)
    # ratio-symmetric: a machine at target, at 2x target and at 1/2 target score 0, -t, -t
    return -np.tanh(np.abs(np.log(post) - np.log(target)))
features.measures: Negative absolute log-ratio between a machine's post-assignment load and the projected final average load (relative rather than absolute distance).

features.name: two_step_lookahead_makespan
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative predicted makespan after this job plus one lookahead job (mean size / high quantile of past sizes) placed greedily on the least loaded machine."""
    m = len(loads)
    job = float(job)
    if past_jobs.size > 0:
        mean_past = float(np.mean(past_jobs))
        hi = float(np.quantile(past_jobs, 0.9))
    else:
        mean_past = job
        hi = job

    L = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    idx = np.arange(m)
    # V[i, j] = load of machine j after placing the arriving job on machine i
    V = L[None, :] + job * np.eye(m)

    k = V.argmin(axis=1)                 # least loaded machine after this placement
    Vk = V[idx, k]
    Vm = V.copy()
    Vm[idx, k] = -np.inf                 # max load ignoring the least loaded machine
    max_excl = Vm.max(axis=1)

    scale = float(V.max()) + abs(job) + max(abs(mean_past), abs(hi)) + 1e-9
    out = np.empty((m, 2))
    for c, nxt in enumerate((mean_past, hi)):
        makespan = np.maximum(max_excl, Vk + nxt)   # lookahead job goes to the emptiest
        out[:, c] = -makespan / scale

    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(out, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=-1.0), -1.0, 1.0)
features.measures: Negative predicted makespan after this job plus one lookahead job (mean size / high quantile of past sizes) placed greedily on the least loaded machine.

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative absolute distance of a machine's post-placement load from the median post-placement load (robust central tendency), scaled by the load spread."""
    post = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float) + float(job)

features.name: reserve_pool_for_future_big_jobs
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Reserve-pool signal: +1 for non-reserved machines, -1 for machines needed as a future-big-job pool, zero when no reserve is needed or the current job is big."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    m = loads.size
    zeros = np.zeros(m, dtype=float)
    past = np.asarray(past_jobs, dtype=float)

    if past.size < 8 or m < 2:
        return zeros

    scale = float(np.partition(past, past.size // 4)[past.size // 4])
    scale = max(scale, 1e-9)
    big = 4.0 * scale

    if job > big:
        return zeros

    frac_big = float(np.mean(past > big))
    R = int(np.clip(round(jobs_left * frac_big), 0, m - 2))
    if R < 1:
        return zeros

    cut = float(np.partition(loads, R - 1)[R - 1])
    s = 0.05 * (abs(cut) + scale) + 1e-9
    return np.clip(np.tanh((loads - cut) / s), -1.0, 1.0)

idea.hypothesis: f001 is exactly least-loaded greedy (its projected target is identical for every candidate, so it collapses to -load). Small jobs therefore keep occupying near-empty machines, and a later large job lands on a machine that already holds one. If small jobs are actively pushed onto the already-loaded (non-reserved) machines, a pool of near-empty machines survives for the big jobs still expected, and bimodal stops paying two large jobs on one machine.
idea.feature: One column, zero unless a reserve is needed and the current job is small. past = past_jobs as float; if past.size < 8 return zeros(m). scale = 25th percentile of past (np.partition(past, past.size//4)[past.size//4], floor 1e-9); big = 4*scale; if job > big return zeros(m); frac_big = mean(past > big); R = clip(round(jobs_left*frac_big), 0, m-2); if R < 1 return zeros(m). cut = float(np.partition(loads, R-1)[R-1]) (the R-th smallest load = the boundary of the reserved pool). s = 0.05*(abs(cut) + scale) + 1e-9; return np.clip(np.tanh((loads - cut)/s), -1, 1), i.e. machines inside the reserve score -1, working machines +1.
idea.lesson: f006 reserve_emptiest_machine_for_big_jobs was discarded as a duplicate of f001 because it never conditioned on the arriving job's size, so the reserve was never actually exercised; here the reserve is only enforced for small jobs.

features.coder_note: The code computes a smooth reserve-pool score for each machine: zero unless at least 8 past jobs exist, a nonzero reserve size \(R\) is predicted from the observed fraction of “big” jobs and remaining arrivals, and the arriving job is not itself big; otherwise it uses the \(R\)-th smallest current …
features.measures: Reserve-pool signal: +1 for non-reserved machines, -1 for machines needed as a future-big-job pool, zero when no reserve is needed or the current job is big.

features.name: scale_free_peak_at_mean_load
features.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Peak score exp(-|post-load - mean post-load| / (std(post) + |job| + 1e-9)), clipped to (0,1]."""
    post = loads + job
    mu = float(post.mean())
    scale = float(post.std()) + abs(float(job)) + 1e-9
    return np.clip(np.exp(-np.abs(post - mu) / scale), 0.0, 1.0)

idea.hypothesis: Every feature that is monotone in loads (including all of f001-f011) ranks candidates identically to least-loaded, which is why the ledger is one big duplicate group. A peak-at-the-mean score, normalised by the decision's own spread and the job size, is genuinely non-monotone: for small jobs it keeps them on machines already near the mean instead of dragging them onto a near-empty machine, while for a large job the emptiest machine is the one that lands nearest the mean, so the big-job behaviour is unchanged.
idea.feature: post = loads + job; mu = float(post.mean()); scale = float(post.std()) + abs(job) + 1e-9; return np.clip(np.exp(-np.abs(post - mu)/scale), 0, 1) (one column, in (0,1], scale-free in load units).

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Two indicator columns: 1 if a machine is exactly idle (load <= 1e-12), 1 if its load <= 0.5*job."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    c1 = (loads <= 1e-12).astype(float)
    c2 = (loads <= 0.5 * job).astype(float)
    return np.stack([c1, c2], axis=1)

idea.hypothesis: The champion only ever prefers a machine by however much less it is loaded, so an essentially empty machine and a one-unit-lighter machine score almost the same; a sharp indicator of idle/very light machines makes the early use of all m machines a first-order effect rather than a tie-break, which should show up as a smaller final load spread if the mechanism matters at all.
idea.feature: Two columns: c1 = (loads <= 1e-12) as float (exactly idle machine); c2 = (loads <= 0.5*job) as float (machine still light relative to this job). Return np.stack([c1, c2], axis=1); no other terms.
idea.lesson: f001 is a monotone re-expression of least-loaded, so the only untested part of 'spread the load early' is the saturation: how much a lightly loaded machine is preferred over an idle one.

features.coder_note: The code computes, per machine, a hard 1/0 flag for "exactly idle" and a hard 1/0 flag for "still light relative to the arriving job" (load ≤ half the job), returning them as two columns exactly as specified with no other terms.

nodes.title: Least-loaded greedy
nodes.description: Score each machine by the negative of its current load, so the arriving job always goes to the emptiest machine (classic Graham list scheduling).

nodes.title: Convex load penalty
nodes.description: Score by a superlinear penalty on current load (e.g. -(loads/max)^2) so already-heavy machines are avoided more sharply than a linear rule.

nodes.title: Balance-to-target
nodes.description: Score by how close loads+job is to the fair share (total+job)/m, i.e. -|loads+job-target|, aiming every machine at the same finish level.

nodes.title: Remaining-work projection
nodes.description: Use jobs_left and the mean past job size to project each machine's final load and prefer machines below their projected fair share.

nodes.title: Idle-machine spreading
nodes.description: Score machines that are still empty or very lightly loaded (indicator or reciprocal of load) to force use of all m machines early.

nodes.title: One-sided slack
nodes.description: Penalise only machines that would exceed the fair share after this job (min(0, target-loads-job)), ignoring how far below target they are.

nodes.title: Distribution-scaled load
nodes.description: Scale the load comparison by observed job statistics (max or mean of past_jobs) so the rule adapts to the family's job-size scale.

nodes.title: Rank-normalized load position
nodes.description: Score each machine by its within-decision rank / standardized deviation of post-placement load (nothing but relative position, divided by the spread of loads), so the rule is invariant to load scale and family job-size regime.

nodes.title: Big-job conditional fit-to-max
nodes.description: If the arriving job is large relative to past_max or past mean, minimise the resulting max load (best fit); otherwise use least-loaded — a nonlinear switch instead of one linear target.

nodes.title: Reserve empty machines for large jobs
nodes.description: Penalise placing jobs on machines whose load is still far below the projected large-job size, keeping a pool of near-empty machines available so each future big job gets its own machine (matches the m-th/(m+1)-th largest term of the bound).
